newsitem.title: USA: N.C. firm agrees to settle discrimination suit.
newsitem.headline: N.C. firm agrees to settle discrimination suit.

text.p: An aviation maintenance company accused by the U.S. Labor Department of allowing a climate hostile to women and minorities has agreed to pay $242,600 to settle the dispute, federal officials said Thursday.
The Labor Department had said 42 employees of Timco of Greensboro, N.C., were either fired, forced to quit or denied promotions as a result of sexual and racial discrimination.
Timco President Charles Bell disputed the federal agency's contention that incidents at his company were "egregious and offensive."
He said he reached the settlement to be sure "everyone was treated equitably and fairly."

Under the settlement, six workers will get their jobs back. The company also agreed to pay $140,000 in back wages and $102,000 for training and other corrective measures. Only 11 of the 42 people allegedly mistreated were cited in the settlement, Bell said.

The Labor Department said its yearlong investigation turned up evidence that an employee threatened to rape and beat a black woman. Other instances involved an employee raffling a knife embossed with a racist logo and another turning his hood around to look like a member of the racist Ku Klux Klan.
Bell said the employees were punished. The one who threatened to rape a co-worker said his remarks were meant in jest. He was required to attend sensitivity training.
The company employs 1,300 people at Piedmont Triad International Airport in Greensboro.
